steps: Create the namespace with `kubectl create namespace exam-sandbox`.
Verify it exists and is Active with `kubectl get namespace exam-sandbox`.
title: Create a namespace
instructions: Create a namespace named `exam-sandbox`.
solution: kubectl create namespace exam-sandbox
resource: kubectl get namespace exam-sandbox --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: Namespaces isolate namespaced API resources.

steps: List nodes with `kubectl get nodes` and choose one. The solution commands select the first node automatically.
Apply the label with `kubectl label node <node-name> exam=ready --overwrite`.
Verify your node appears in `kubectl get nodes -l exam=ready --show-labels`.
title: Label a node
instructions: Add the label `exam=ready` to any node.
solution:
node=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl label node "$node" exam=ready --overwrite
resource: kubectl get nodes -l exam=ready -o json
explanation: Node labels can be used to select nodes for scheduling.

steps: Find a worker with `kubectl get nodes`. The solution commands select a node without the control-plane label.
Taint it with `kubectl taint node <worker-name> exam=reserved:NoSchedule --overwrite`.
Cordon it with `kubectl cordon <worker-name>`.
Run `kubectl describe node <worker-name>` and confirm the taint and `Unschedulable: true`.
title: Taint and cordon a node
instructions: Add the taint `exam=reserved:NoSchedule` to one node, and mark one node unschedulable (cordon). New Pods that do not tolerate the taint must no longer be placed on the tainted node.
solution:
worker=$(kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.labels["node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane"] == null)][0].metadata.name')
kubectl taint node "$worker" exam=reserved:NoSchedule --overwrite
kubectl cordon "$worker"
resource: kubectl get nodes -o json

checks.description: A node carries the reservation taint

explanation: Taints repel Pods unless they tolerate them, while cordon marks a node unschedulable without evicting running Pods. Both are reversible with `kubectl uncordon` and `kubectl taint nodes <node> exam=reserved:NoSchedule-`.

steps: Choose a worker and find its InternalIP with `kubectl get nodes -o wide`.
SSH to the worker and write the Pod manifest shown below to `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml` using sudo. The kubelet watches this directory; do not use kubectl apply for a static Pod.
On the controller, run `kubectl get pods -o wide`. Confirm a mirror Pod named `static-web-<node-name>` appears on the chosen worker.
title: Run a static Pod
instructions: On one of the worker nodes, create a static Pod manifest named `static-web` using image `nginx:1.27`. The kubelet must run a Pod named `static-web-<node-name>`. SSH access to the worker nodes is configured from the lab terminal; do not run it on the control-plane node.
solution:
worker=$(kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.labels["node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane"] == null)][0].metadata.name')
ip=$(kubectl get node "$worker" -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
ssh "$ip" 'sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml >/dev/null' <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.27
YAML
resource: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json

checks.description: Static Pod is registered with the API server

explanation: The kubelet watches its static Pod manifest directory (`/etc/kubernetes/manifests` by default) and creates a mirror Pod so the workload is visible to the API server.

steps: Run this task on the control-plane node. Create `/opt/backup` with sudo.
Use `ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl` against `https://127.0.0.1:2379` with the CA, server certificate, and key under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`, as shown below.
Save the snapshot to `/opt/backup/etcd.db`, then confirm it is nonempty with `sudo ls -lh /opt/backup/etcd.db`.
title: Back up etcd
instructions: On the control-plane node, create an etcd snapshot and save it as `/opt/backup/etcd.db`. The `etcdctl` client is installed and the etcd certificates are in `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`. The snapshot must be a readable etcd backup.
solution:
sudo -n mkdir -p /opt/backup
sudo -n env ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /opt/backup/etcd.db
resource: sudo -n etcdctl snapshot status /opt/backup/etcd.db -w json 2>/dev/null || echo '{}'
explanation: `etcdctl snapshot save` stores a consistent copy of the etcd key space. Restoring it requires stopping the API server and etcd, then running `etcdctl snapshot restore` into a new data directory.

steps: Create the Pod with `kubectl -n exam-workloads run web --image=nginx:1.27`.
Verify its image and status with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe pod web`.
title: Create a pod
instructions: In namespace `exam-workloads`, create a pod named `web` using image `nginx:1.27`.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads run web --image=nginx:1.27
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get pod web --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A Pod specification declares its container image.

steps: Create the Deployment with `kubectl -n exam-workloads create deployment api --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2`.
Wait with `kubectl -n exam-workloads rollout status deployment/api`, then check that `kubectl -n exam-workloads get deployment api` reports two available replicas.
title: Create a deployment
instructions: In namespace `exam-workloads`, create a deployment named `api` using image `nginx:1.27` with 2 replicas.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads create deployment api --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get deployment api --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: The Deployment template supplies the image and its replica count defines the desired scale.

steps: Update the `web` container with `kubectl -n exam-workloads set image deployment/rollout web=nginx:1.26`.
Wait for the update with `kubectl -n exam-workloads rollout status deployment/rollout`.
Undo it with `kubectl -n exam-workloads rollout undo deployment/rollout` and wait for rollout status again.
Verify `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe deployment rollout` shows `nginx:1.27` again.
title: Roll back a deployment
instructions: The Deployment `rollout` in namespace `exam-workloads` runs `nginx:1.27`. Update it to `nginx:1.26`, wait for the rollout, then roll back to the previous revision. When you are done it must run `nginx:1.27` again and report at least 3 revisions.
solution:
kubectl -n exam-workloads set image deployment/rollout web=nginx:1.26
kubectl -n exam-workloads rollout status deployment/rollout --timeout=180s
kubectl -n exam-workloads rollout undo deployment/rollout
kubectl -n exam-workloads rollout status deployment/rollout --timeout=180s
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get deployment rollout --ignore-not-found -o json

checks.description: A new revision was rolled out

explanation: Each Pod template change creates a ReplicaSet revision. `kubectl rollout undo` reuses the previous ReplicaSet and records the rollback as a new revision.

steps: Define a Pod named `pipeline` in `exam-workloads` with an init container named `prepare`, using `busybox:1.36` and running `sh -c 'sleep 2'`.
Add regular containers named `app` using `nginx:1.27` and `log-sidecar` using `busybox:1.36`; keep the sidecar running with `sh -c 'tail -f /dev/null'`.
Apply the manifest below. Verify with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe pod pipeline`: the init container should complete and both regular containers should run.
title: Build a multi-container Pod
instructions: Create a Pod named `pipeline` in `exam-workloads` with an init container `prepare` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c "sleep 2"`) and two containers: `app` (image `nginx:1.27`) and `log-sidecar` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c "tail -f /dev/null"`). The Pod must reach the Running phase.
solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pipeline
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: prepare
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 2"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
    - name: log-sidecar
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -f /dev/null"]
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get pod pipeline --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: Init containers run to completion before application containers start, while sidecar containers run alongside the main container in the same Pod.

steps: Define a one-replica Deployment named `resource-demo` in `exam-workloads`, using `nginx:1.27`.
Set the container requests to CPU `100m` and memory `128Mi`, and limits to CPU `500m` and memory `256Mi`.
Apply the manifest below. Verify requests and limits with `kubectl -n exam-workloads get deployment resource-demo -o yaml`.
title: Set resource requests and limits
instructions: Create a Deployment named `resource-demo` in `exam-workloads` with one replica, image `nginx:1.27`, and container resources requesting `100m` CPU and `128Mi` memory with limits of `500m` CPU and `256Mi` memory.
solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: resource-demo
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: resource-demo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 256Mi
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get deployment resource-demo --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: Requests drive scheduling decisions; limits cap how much a container may consume before it is throttled or OOM-killed.

steps: Create the quota with `kubectl -n exam-workloads create quota limit-pods --hard=pods=20`.
Apply the LimitRange below, named `default-limits`, with container defaults of CPU `200m` and memory `256Mi`, and default requests of CPU `100m` and memory `128Mi`.
Verify both policies with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe quota limit-pods` and `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe limitrange default-limits`.
title: Limit a namespace
instructions: In namespace `exam-workloads`, create a ResourceQuota named `limit-pods` limiting pods to 20, and a LimitRange named `default-limits` that applies a Container default limit of `200m` CPU and `256Mi` memory with a default request of `100m` CPU and `128Mi` memory.
solution:
kubectl -n exam-workloads create quota limit-pods --hard=pods=20
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 200m
        memory: 256Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get resourcequota,limitrange -o json

checks.expression: any(.items[]?; .kind == "LimitRange" and .metadata.name == "default-limits" and any(.spec.limits[]?; .type == "Container" and .default.cpu == "200m" and .default.memory == "256Mi" and .defaultRequest.cpu == "100m" and .defaultRequest.memory == "128Mi"))

explanation: A ResourceQuota caps the total resources a namespace may consume, while a LimitRange supplies defaults and bounds for individual containers.

steps: Create the cluster-scoped class with `kubectl create priorityclass exam-critical --value=100000`. Do not make it a global default.
Verify the value and default flag with `kubectl get priorityclass exam-critical -o yaml`.
title: Create a PriorityClass
instructions: Create a PriorityClass named `exam-critical` with the value `100000`. It must not be the cluster default PriorityClass.
solution: kubectl create priorityclass exam-critical --value=100000
resource: kubectl get priorityclass exam-critical --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: The scheduler prefers Pods with a higher PriorityClass value; `globalDefault` would apply it to every Pod that omits a class.

steps: Create the Job with `kubectl -n exam-workloads create job hello --image=busybox:1.36 -- echo hello`.
Wait with `kubectl -n exam-workloads wait --for=condition=complete job/hello --timeout=120s`, then check `kubectl -n exam-workloads logs job/hello`.
title: Create a Job
instructions: Create a Job named `hello` in namespace `exam-workloads` using image `busybox:1.36` which runs `echo hello`.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads create job hello --image=busybox:1.36 -- echo hello
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get job hello --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A Job runs a workload to completion with the specified command.

steps: Create the CronJob using `busybox:1.36`, schedule `*/5 * * * *`, and command `echo hello`, as shown below. Quote the schedule so the shell does not expand its asterisks.
Verify the schedule, image, and command with `kubectl -n exam-workloads get cronjob periodic -o yaml`. You do not need to wait five minutes for a scheduled run.
title: Schedule a Job
instructions: Create a CronJob named `periodic` in `exam-workloads` using `busybox:1.36`, scheduled every five minutes, running `echo hello`.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads create cronjob periodic --image=busybox:1.36 --schedule='*/5 * * * *' -- echo hello
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get cronjob periodic --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A CronJob uses a cron schedule to create Jobs from a template.

steps: Create the ConfigMap with `kubectl -n exam-workloads create configmap settings --from-literal=mode=production`.
Verify its data contains `mode: production` with `kubectl -n exam-workloads get configmap settings -o yaml`.
title: Create a ConfigMap
instructions: In namespace `exam-workloads`, create a ConfigMap named `settings` with key `mode` set to `production`.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads create configmap settings --from-literal=mode=production
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get configmap settings --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential key-value configuration.

steps: Create the Secret with `kubectl -n exam-workloads create secret generic credentials --from-literal=username=operator`.
Verify the stored value with `kubectl -n exam-workloads get secret credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d`; it should print `operator`.
title: Create a Secret
instructions: In namespace `exam-workloads`, create a generic Secret named `credentials` with key `username` set to `operator`.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads create secret generic credentials --from-literal=username=operator
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get secret credentials --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: Secret values are stored base64-encoded in the API and should be handled as sensitive data.

steps: Create the account with `kubectl -n exam-workloads create serviceaccount observer`.
Verify it exists in the correct namespace with `kubectl -n exam-workloads get serviceaccount observer`.
title: Create a ServiceAccount
instructions: Create a ServiceAccount named `observer` in namespace `exam-workloads`.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads create serviceaccount observer
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get serviceaccount observer --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A ServiceAccount provides an identity for workloads in its namespace.

steps: Define the cluster-scoped PV `exam-pv` with capacity `1Gi`, access mode `ReadWriteOnce`, storage class `exam-local`, and hostPath `/tmp/exam-data`.
Define the PVC `exam-claim` in `exam-workloads`, requesting `1Gi` with matching access mode and storage class.
Apply the two-resource manifest below. Run `kubectl get pv exam-pv` and `kubectl -n exam-workloads get pvc exam-claim` and confirm both are Bound to each other.
title: Bind a persistent volume
instructions: Create a PersistentVolume named `exam-pv` with capacity `1Gi`, access mode `ReadWriteOnce`, storage class `exam-local` and hostPath `/tmp/exam-data`. Create a PersistentVolumeClaim named `exam-claim` in `exam-workloads` requesting `1Gi` with the same access mode and class, and make sure it binds to `exam-pv`.
solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: exam-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: exam-local
  hostPath:
    path: /tmp/exam-data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: exam-claim
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: exam-local
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get pv,pvc -o json

checks.description: Volume capacity, mode and backing path
checks.expression: any(.items[]?; .kind == "PersistentVolume" and .metadata.name == "exam-pv" and .spec.capacity.storage == "1Gi" and (.spec.accessModes | index("ReadWriteOnce") != null) and .spec.storageClassName == "exam-local" and .spec.hostPath.path == "/tmp/exam-data")

any(.items[]?; .kind == "PersistentVolumeClaim" and .metadata.name == "exam-claim" and .spec.resources.requests.storage == "1Gi" and .spec.storageClassName == "exam-local" and (.spec.accessModes | index("ReadWriteOnce") != null))

checks.description: Claim is bound to the volume

explanation: The control plane binds a claim to a volume whose capacity, access modes and storage class satisfy the request; `volumeName` pins a specific volume.

steps: Check the existing ConfigMap with `kubectl -n exam-workloads get configmap exam-material`.
Define Pod `config-mount` using `nginx:1.27`. Add a volume referencing `exam-material` and mount that volume at `/etc/exam` in the container.
Apply the manifest below. Verify the mount with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe pod config-mount` and inspect the files with `kubectl -n exam-workloads exec config-mount -- ls /etc/exam`.
title: Mount a ConfigMap
instructions: Create a Pod named `config-mount` in `exam-workloads` using image `nginx:1.27` that mounts the existing ConfigMap `exam-material` as a volume named `config` at `/etc/exam`. The Pod must be running.
solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-mount
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.27
      volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/exam
  volumes:
    - name: config
      configMap:
        name: exam-material
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get pod config-mount --ignore-not-found -o json

checks.description: Volume is mounted into the container

explanation: ConfigMap data can be projected into a Pod as files; a volume must be declared and then mounted into a container.

steps: Expose the Deployment with `kubectl -n exam-workloads expose deployment service-target --name=api --port=80 --target-port=80`. The default Service type is ClusterIP.
Verify the type, ports, and selector with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe service api`.
title: Expose a deployment
instructions: Expose the existing deployment `service-target` in namespace `exam-workloads` as a ClusterIP service named `api` on port 80 targeting port 80.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads expose deployment service-target --name=api --port=80 --target-port=80
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get service api --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A ClusterIP Service routes port 80 to Pods selected by the deployment label.

steps: Expose the Deployment with `kubectl -n exam-workloads expose deployment service-target --name=web-nodeport --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=80`.
Verify the type and allocated node port with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe service web-nodeport`. Kubernetes chooses an available node port automatically.
title: Create a NodePort service
instructions: Expose the deployment `service-target` in `exam-workloads` again, this time as a NodePort Service named `web-nodeport` on port 80 targeting container port 80.
solution: kubectl -n exam-workloads expose deployment service-target --name=web-nodeport --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=80
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get service web-nodeport --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A NodePort Service allocates a port on every node and forwards traffic to the selected Pods.

steps: Define Ingress `web` in `exam-workloads` with a rule for host `exam.local`.
Route path `/` with pathType `Prefix` to Service `exam-backend` on port `80`, as shown below.

Apply the manifest, then verify the routing rule with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe ingress web`. An Ingress controller is needed for actual traffic routing; this task checks the resource configuration.
title: Route traffic with an Ingress
instructions: Create an Ingress named `web` in `exam-workloads` that routes requests for host `exam.local` to the existing Service `exam-backend` on port 80. Use the path `/` with pathType `Prefix`. This lab has no ingress controller, so only the resource configuration is checked.
solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  rules:
    - host: exam.local
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: exam-backend
                port:
                  number: 80
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get ingress web --ignore-not-found -o json

checks.description: Host routes to the backend service

explanation: An Ingress is an API-level routing rule; an ingress controller (not installed here) is what actually programs a proxy from those rules.

steps: Define NetworkPolicy `deny-ingress` in `exam-workloads` with `podSelector: {}` to select every Pod.
Set `policyTypes` to `Ingress` and omit ingress allow rules. Apply the manifest below.
Verify with `kubectl -n exam-workloads describe networkpolicy deny-ingress`. The default Flannel CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy; this task checks the policy configuration only.
title: Default deny ingress
instructions: Create a NetworkPolicy named `deny-ingress` in `exam-workloads` selecting all Pods and specifying default-deny ingress. The default Flannel lab CNI does not enforce policies; this task checks the resource configuration.
solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-ingress
  namespace: exam-workloads
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
YAML
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get networkpolicy deny-ingress --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A policy selecting all Pods with ingress and no allow rules specifies default-deny ingress. Enforcement requires a policy-capable CNI.

steps: Scale the Deployment with `kubectl -n kube-system scale deployment/coredns --replicas=3`.
Wait with `kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deployment/coredns --timeout=180s`.
Verify `kubectl -n kube-system get deployment coredns` reports three ready and available replicas.
title: Scale CoreDNS
instructions: Scale the CoreDNS Deployment in `kube-system` to three replicas and wait until all three are available.
solution:
kubectl -n kube-system scale deployment/coredns --replicas=3
kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deployment/coredns --timeout=180s
resource: kubectl -n kube-system get deployment coredns --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: Cluster DNS is served by the CoreDNS Deployment; running more than one replica removes the single point of failure.

steps: Inspect `kubectl -n exam-repair describe deployment broken-web` and the associated Pod events to identify the incorrect image.
Fix the `web` container with `kubectl -n exam-repair set image deployment/broken-web web=nginx:1.27`.
Wait with `kubectl -n exam-repair rollout status deployment/broken-web --timeout=180s`, then verify its replicas are available.
title: Troubleshoot a deployment
instructions: The `broken-web` deployment in namespace `exam-repair` cannot start. Fix its image to `nginx:1.27` and ensure it has one available replica.
solution:
kubectl -n exam-repair set image deployment/broken-web web=nginx:1.27
kubectl -n exam-repair rollout status deployment/broken-web --timeout=180s
resource: kubectl -n exam-repair get deployment broken-web --ignore-not-found -o json
explanation: A valid container image lets the Deployment controller create an available replica; `kubectl describe` and Pod events show the image pull failure.

steps: Compare `kubectl -n exam-repair get service broken-endpoints -o yaml` with `kubectl -n exam-repair get pods --show-labels` to find the selector mismatch.
Patch the Service selector to `app: endpoint-target` with the command below.
Verify the Service selects the intended Pods and has endpoint addresses with `kubectl -n exam-repair get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=broken-endpoints`.
title: Repair a service
instructions: The Service `broken-endpoints` in `exam-repair` has no endpoints, so traffic never reaches the Pods of the `endpoint-target` Deployment. Repair the Service so that it has at least one ready endpoint.
solution: kubectl -n exam-repair patch service broken-endpoints --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"endpoint-target"}}}'
resource: kubectl -n exam-repair get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=broken-endpoints -o json

checks.description: Service has at least one ready endpoint

explanation: Endpoints are generated from the Service selector; a selector that matches no Pod labels leaves the Service without backends.

steps: Inspect `kubectl -n exam-repair describe deployment crashing` and its Pod logs to identify the command that exits immediately.
Replace the first container command with `sh -c 'sleep 3600'` using the JSON patch below, so the container keeps running.
Wait with `kubectl -n exam-repair rollout status deployment/crashing --timeout=180s`, then confirm the replacement Pod is Ready.
title: Recover a crashing workload
instructions: The Deployment `crashing` in `exam-repair` never becomes ready because its container exits immediately. Fix the workload so that exactly one replica is available.
solution:
kubectl -n exam-repair patch deployment crashing --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/command","value":["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]}]'
kubectl -n exam-repair rollout status deployment/crashing --timeout=180s

steps: Create Role `pod-reader` in `exam-workloads`, granting only `get`, `list`, and `watch` on `pods`.

title: Grant namespaced permissions
instructions: Create a Role named `pod-reader` in `exam-workloads` allowing get, list and watch on Pods, and bind it to ServiceAccount `binding-observer` in the same namespace with a RoleBinding named `read-pods`.
solution:
kubectl -n exam-workloads create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n exam-workloads create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=exam-workloads:binding-observer
resource: kubectl -n exam-workloads get role,rolebinding -o json

checks.description: RoleBinding connects the Role to the ServiceAccount
checks.expression: any(.items[]?; .kind == "RoleBinding" and .metadata.name == "read-pods" and .roleRef.kind == "Role" and .roleRef.name == "pod-reader" and any(.subjects[]?; .kind == "ServiceAccount" and .name == "binding-observer" and .namespace == "exam-workloads"))

explanation: A Role lists permissions inside a namespace; a RoleBinding grants them to users, groups or ServiceAccounts. `kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:exam-workloads:binding-observer list pods` verifies the result.

steps: Create ClusterRole `node-reader`, granting only `get`, `list`, and `watch` on the cluster-scoped `nodes` resource.

title: Grant cluster-wide permissions
instructions: Create a ClusterRole named `node-reader` allowing get, list and watch on nodes, and bind it to ServiceAccount `cluster-observer` in `exam-workloads` with a ClusterRoleBinding named `node-reader`.
solution:
kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding node-reader --clusterrole=node-reader --serviceaccount=exam-workloads:cluster-observer
